name: Xong / Fenghuang Xong
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sposato, Adam. 2015. A Grammar of Xong. PhD dissertation, State University of New York at Buffalo. xv+659 pp. (the Internet Archive snapshot of the UB Linguistics alumni-dissertations PDF; published rev. as Sposato 2021, Mouton Grammar Library 84.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 3.5.1 'Overview', p. 94; sec. 3.6 'A note on non-tonal suprasegmental phenomena', p. 117; sec. 1.4 'Directions for future research', p. 9; sec. 3.5.2.1; ch. 3 opening
catalog_quote: In all varieties of Fenghuang Xong, tone is primarily a syllable-level phenomenon. With only a few exceptions (see Section 3.6), each syllable produced in isolation in any variety of Fenghuang Xong will be accompanied by one of eight lexically specified tones. These “tones” are not simply specified pitch heights or contours; rather, they are each a complex “bundle” consisting of a specified pitch height, a specified pitch contour, and a specified phonation type (e.g. modal, breathy, creaky). ... However, while the basic suprasegmental characteristics of each syllable are largely determined by the syllable’s tone, there appears to be an additional intonational system which is further overlaid over the Xong tonal system. ... [p. 117] This intonational system appears to make use of (at least) distinctive pitch heights, distinctive pitch contours, and distinctive durations, and it appears to operate at the level of polysyllabic phonological phrases rather than at the level of individual syllables. [p. 9] Xong appears to possess at least two distinct suprasegmental systems: a syllable-level system of lexically specified tones, many of which involve distinctive phonation types in addition to distinctive pitch heights and contours (see Section 3.5), and a phrase-level system of intonation contours overlaid on those tones (Section 3.6).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Xong is described as fully tonal: every syllable (bar a handful of toneless particles/interjections) carries one of eight lexical tone-phonation bundles; the only other suprasegmental system the author identifies is phrase-level intonation. No word-level stress or accent is described anywhere in the grammar; the notion is simply absent.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless particles and interjections (sec. 3.6, 9.2.1, 11.3) whose pitch/duration vary with sentence modality; emphatic/focus 'exaggeration' of tones; utterance-final pitch fall. Separately, Ratliff 2010:199 (held) states family-wide that Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes 'are unstressed' (Jiwei Qo Xiong qo1- etc.), the only explicit stress remark found bearing on this language.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone = syllable/lexical level; intonation = polysyllabic phonological phrase/utterance level; monosyllables elicited in isolation are treated as full utterances subject to utterance-final fall. Variety: Yankan Village (La'ershan), Fenghuang County.
new_statements.identity_note: Sposato 2015 describes 'Fenghuang Xong', chiefly the variety of Yankan Village (La'ershan Town, Fenghuang County, W Hunan), with notes on Shanjiang and Zhuigaolai varieties; all fall under Western Xiangxi Miao [west2430 / ISO mmr] (the Jiwei standard, Huayuan County, is the same language; Sposato notes Jiwei has 6 tones vs 8 in Fenghuang and no reported toneless syllables). Ratliff 2010's statement is family-level (Hmong-Mien) with Jiwei 'Qo Xiong' examples, not a Xong-specific description.

sources.note: Nothing: 'stress' never used phonologically in 674 pp. Ch.3: every syllable bears one of 8 lexical tones (sec.3.5.1 p.94) except a few toneless particles/interjections; sec.3.6 p.117 describes only a phrase-level intonation system (utterance-final fall, emphatic tone exaggeration, interrogative intonation); sec.1.4 p.9 'at least two distinct suprasegmental systems': syllable-level tone + phrase-level intonation. Nominal prefixes (ghaob- etc.) carry full tone -b and undergo regular sandhi; no reduction/stress remarks.

sources.note: Per Sposato 2015: 43 (who read the 1947 original): the language chapter's phonology (1947: 421-432) claims that 'only five tones are distinguished in their Xong consultants' speech (1947: 431)', which Sposato finds surprising since every other description of Fenghuang Xong has at least seven; it also gives a single (retroflex) sibilant-affricate series and no unaspirated prenasalized stops. Earliest (1933 fieldwork) tone record of Fenghuang Xong; n_tones = 5 per that report. Not read by me.
